records.name: Indiana
records.current_summary: A February 2026 per-state legal-risk assessment placed Indiana 'among the harshest anti-trans states in the country', citing its 2026 identity-document law and escalating bathroom restrictions as the drivers of its adult-risk rating; the July 2026 edition keeps it in the worst-state group.

sources.claim: Erin In The Morning 'Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map' (February 2026): per-state legal-risk grading of anti-trans law; states that Indiana's 2026 ID policy 'now places it among the harshest anti-trans states in the country', with bathroom-ban escalation driving adult risk and Kansas added to the 'Do Not Travel' category.

Indiana residents lost the option to change their gender marker on driver's licenses or other identification cards when the Bureau of Motor Vehicles' new ban took effect on Feb. 1, 2026, ending the long-standing route of obtaining such a change through a court-ordered gender change or physician statement. The ban culminates an administrative rule change the BMV initiated; LGBTQ advocates who testified warned it will forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents. The article also reports that pending Indiana Senate Bill 182 would create legal definitions for sex and gender, ban amendments to birth certificates, restrict bathrooms in public schools and restrict housing in prisons. This is the state's 2026 identity-document law the record ties to Indiana's harshest-state rating.

On Jan. 27, 2026, Indiana Senate Republicans approved Senate Bill 182 by a 37-8 party-line vote and sent it to the House; the bill would require public K-12 schools and state universities to designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas for use only by males or females based on their reproductive biology at birth, barring transgender students from facilities matching their gender identity. Author Sen. Liz Brown, R-Fort Wayne, said the proposal lets women 'continue to have their private spaces'; opponents including GenderNexus argued that letting anyone 'directly or indirectly injured' sue a school over an alleged violation would encourage harassment-style enforcement. This documents the escalating bathroom restrictions the record cites as a driver of Indiana's adult-risk rating.

In May 2023 the Indiana Supreme Court declined, in split votes, to hear two cases of transgender girls seeking to change the gender on their birth certificates; the denials left appeals-court rulings standing that trial courts lack authority to grant such changes unless the General Assembly codifies them. One case involved a nine-year-old transgender girl whose birth certificate's male designation allowed her school to restrict her bathroom access. This is the court outcome that kept Indiana's birth-certificate gender-marker change off limits ahead of the 2026 identity-document law.

flags: criminal-charge exposure for bathroom use has been flagged since 2023 (sole source unverifiable)

records.name: Utah
records.current_summary: Utah's HB 257 (January 2024) was the first statewide bathroom ban in the country reaching trans adults, not only school facilities; it remains in force, alongside birth-certificate and surgery requirements for amended markers and a complaint channel for objecting officials.   In May 2025 Utah became the first state to explicitly prohibit flying LGBTQ flags at government buildings and schools (fines up to $500 per day), with similar flag bans following in other states — its Pride organisation calls the state's legislative record the nation's most anti-LGBT.

sources.claim: Guardian report (29 May 2025) on Pride 2025 in the US: on 7 May Utah became the first state to explicitly prohibit flying LGBTQ+ flags at government buildings and schools, with fines of $500 a day; Utah Pride's executive director says the state 'leads the nation in anti-LGBTQ legislation'; similar flag bans were signed in Idaho and Montana, while Salt Lake City issued counter-flags and Boise made the pride flag an official city flag.

On Jan. 30, 2024, Republican Gov. Spencer Cox signed HB 257, making Utah the latest state to regulate bathroom access for transgender people; the law requires people to use bathrooms and locker rooms in public schools and government-owned buildings that match their sex assigned at birth. Under the legislation transgender people can defend themselves against complaints by showing documentation of gender-affirming care, and new government buildings must include single-occupant bathrooms. NBC reported at least 10 other states had passed similar bathroom-regulation laws by then and quoted the ACLU of Utah opposing the bill for risking discriminatory enforcement. This is the dated enactment of the adult-reaching bathroom ban the record attributes to HB 257.

Official Utah Legislature page for HB 257 ('Sex-based Designations for Privacy, Anti-bullying, and Women's Opportunities'): the bill's action history shows it was introduced Jan. 11, 2024, advanced through House and Senate committee and floor stages across several substitute versions, and the page's last recorded action is '30 Jan 2024, Governor Signed.' Subject tags cover state facilities, K-12 and higher education, and health and human services. Primary state-government confirmation of the bill number, short title and Jan. 30, 2024 signing date.

Star Observer documents the reporting mechanism Utah set up under HB 257: a form through which residents can report transgender people in 'privacy spaces' such as changing rooms and restrooms, with complainants able to choose whether their names are included while the state investigates each 'violation'. The article says the form implements HB 257, 'Sex-Based Designations for Privacy, Anti-Bullying and Women's Opportunities', passed in January 2024, which banned trans Utahns from using bathrooms or competing in a sport that matches their gender identity. This confirms the complaint channel the record lists among Utah's facility-law provisions.

flags: First state to criminalise adult restroom use (HB 257, 2024)
First state to explicitly prohibit LGBTQ flags at government buildings

freshness.fact: Jan 30 2024 bathroom law stands (birth-certificate proof, surgery requirement for amended markers) with 2024 complaint channel for officials; no injunction or repeal found on state page.

Mark Gordon signed two facility measures into law: House Bill 72, the 'Protecting privacy in public spaces act,' covering sex-designated restrooms, showers, sleeping quarters and locker rooms at public facilities, and Senate File 62, 'Sex-designated facilities and public schools,' requiring public school children, pre-kindergarten and up plus charter school students, to use restrooms aligned with sex assigned at birth. records.name: Arkansas
records.current_summary: Arkansas confines trans students to birth-sex school facilities under a March 2023 law (HB 1156) that remains in force and was extended in 2025; its school focus means visitor exposure is narrower than in states with adult-reaching bans.   Its ban on gender-affirming care for minors remains in litigation (en-banc review of an injunction reversal pending), and the July 2026 per-state legal-risk grading lists Arkansas among the worst states.

sources.claim: MAP (Movement Advancement Project) equality-map page cataloguing state bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity; the dossier cites it (via its Feb 2026 citations PDF, also 404 at fetch time) for HB 1156 as a 2023 K-12 facility ban extended in 2025. NOTE: URL returned a 404 at fetch time (MAP has moved the page).

Erin In The Morning, 'Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map: July 2026' (Stonewall News, published 27 Aug 2026): a per-state legal-risk grading of anti-trans law. The adult map lists 'Do Not Travel (FL, ID, KS, TX)' and 'The Worst States (AL, AR, IA, IN, LA, MS, OH, OK, ND, SC, SD, TN, UT, WV, WY)' - this state is in the worst group. The update records Idaho's promotion to 'Do Not Travel' as the fourth such state after its felony bathroom ban (up to 5 years; partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists), Kansas's bounty-hunter civil-suit regime, and a national frame of 'Worst Policies In Effect'.

Wikipedia's LGBTQIA+ rights in Arkansas page records that a bathroom bill became law on 11 April 2023 (Act 619), making Arkansas the fourth state to restrict trans students' use of school bathrooms matching their gender, and that it was amended/extended in 2025. The page also notes Arkansas was the first state (2021) to ban gender-affirming healthcare for trans minors, a law a federal judge enjoined for 'irreparable harm' to minors while litigation continued, and that state law has permitted transgender people to amend birth certificates since 1981. Confirms the record's account of the 2023 school-facility law and the still-litigated care ban.

LGBTQ Nation (March 2021) reported that Arkansas became the first state to ban gender-affirming healthcare for trans youth after the legislature overrode the governor's veto of the ban, which critics at the time called 'the single most extreme anti-trans law to ever pass through a state legislature.' This is the same 2021 care ban whose court challenge the record describes as still in litigation.

records.name: Ohio

An independent July 2026 legal-risk assessment of anti-trans legislation lists Ohio among its 'worst states' group for transgender adults, alongside most of the Deep South and several Plains and Mountain states; the same assessment's frame is 'Worst Policies In Effect' nationally.

sources.claim: Erin In The Morning, 'Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map: July 2026' (Stonewall News, published 27 Aug 2026): a per-state legal-risk grading of anti-trans law. The adult map lists 'Do Not Travel (FL, ID, KS, TX)' and 'The Worst States (AL, AR, IA, IN, LA, MS, OH, OK, ND, SC, SD, TN, UT, WV, WY)' - this state is in the worst group. The update records Idaho's promotion to 'Do Not Travel' as the fourth such state after its felony bathroom ban (up to 5 years; partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists), Kansas's bounty-hunter civil-suit regime, and a national frame of 'Worst Policies In Effect'.

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed the measure on Nov. 27, 2024; under the new law all K-12 schools and colleges must require students to use bathrooms and locker rooms matching the gender on their birth certificates. The article identifies Senate Bill 104 as the legislative vehicle and notes the bill also designates public and private school bathrooms and other facilities such as locker rooms by sex. For this record: dated confirmation of Ohio's 2024 facility-use law as enacted and signed.

AP report that on Nov. 27, 2024 Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed the 'Protect All Students Act,' signing out of public view and over the objections of Democrats, teachers' unions and civil rights groups. The measure requires public and private schools, colleges and universities to designate separate bathrooms, locker rooms and overnight accommodations 'for the exclusive use' of either males or females based on sex assigned at or near birth; it takes effect in 90 days and contains no enforcement mechanism, with sponsor Republican state Sen. Jerry Cirino. Documents the scope (K-12 through college) and 90-day clock of the state's new facility restriction.

Law-firm client alert: on Nov. 27, 2024, Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed Senate Bill 104, officially the 'Protect All Students Act' but widely coined the 'Bathroom Bill,' which outlines specific guidelines and restrictions for the use of restrooms, locker rooms, changing rooms and shower rooms in Ohio schools, with an effective date of Feb. 25, 2025. Independent legal reading of the statute's facility restriction and its implementation timeline for schools and colleges.

'Safe states don't make safer people' (The Needle, July 2026): data essay overlaying the state legal-risk map on Trans Murder Monitoring killings data - legal-risk grades predict how the state behaves, not how people behave toward trans people; every count is an undercount; rates do not line up with the map. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds signed two bills on March 22, 2023: Senate File 538 bars doctors from administering gender-affirming care to anyone under 18 (covering puberty blockers, hormone therapy and transition-related surgeries), and Senate File 482 prevents transgender students from entering school bathrooms or changing rooms that correspond with their gender identities. The restroom restriction applies to multiperson restrooms and locker rooms at public and private elementary and secondary schools and took effect immediately, with single-person facilities available to trans students who obtain written consent from legal guardians. Names both statutes behind this record's Iowa summary.

On March 8, 2019 the Iowa Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Good v. Iowa Dept. of Human Services that the state discriminated against two transgender women by denying their Medicaid claims for transition-related surgery, holding that excluding Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming surgery violates the Iowa Civil Rights Act. Documents the Iowa court carve-back of the state's surgery-coverage ban for adults that this record references.

Tracks the state-court path that kept Medicaid surgery coverage available to transgender adults in Iowa.

KCCI (Des Moines) reporting syndicated by KTVZ: Gov. Kim Reynolds signed SF 482 into law on March 22, 2023, requiring anyone in an Iowa school, including students, staff, parents and visitors, to use only restrooms and other changing areas that correspond with the biological sex listed on their birth certificate, and Iowa school districts are scrambling to comply as the restriction takes effect. States the exact statute and subject scope (everyone on school grounds) behind Iowa's public-facility-use law.

records.name: Florida
records.current_summary: Florida's 2023 law (Fla. Stat. 553.865) makes it a second-degree criminal trespass — up to 60 days — to remain in a public bathroom or changing facility that does not match sex assigned at birth after a government employee orders departure; the ACLU of Florida calls it 'complex, confusing, and vague' and of limited actual coverage, and among at least 14 states with facility restrictions only Florida and Utah criminalise the act itself.  In March 2025 a 20-year-old trans student was arrested using a women's restroom in the State Capitol — believed the first arrest anywhere under a state bathroom ban. A Leon County judge dismissed the charge in June 2025 on speedy-trial grounds after the state missed a 90-day filing deadline; because the arrest was booked as trespass, the ban's constitutionality was never reached. Equality Florida and the Human Rights Campaign have issued named travel advisories warning of risks to trans travellers and movers.  Physical safety is comparatively better than the law suggests: a July 2026 analysis puts Florida's recorded killing rate for trans women at 3.7 per 100k per year, below the average of the worst-law states — itself an undercount floor.

sources.claim: ACLU Florida know-your-rights on the 2023 restroom law (Fla. Stat. 553.865): refusing to leave a sex-segregated restroom or changing facility can be criminal trespass, but the law only applies in buildings owned or leased by the state or local government — state offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons/jails, local immigration detention, state parks and toll-road plazas — and purports to cover all schools, public or private. Private businesses are outside its scope; the ACLU advises fact-specific judgment and legal counsel.

NBC News (2025): Marcy Rheintgen, a 20-year-old trans college student, was arrested at the Florida State Capitol after declaring 'I am here to break the law' and entering a women's restroom — believed to be the first arrest under Florida's transgender bathroom restrictions. She faces a misdemeanor trespass charge punishable by up to 60 days in jail; at least 14 states have adopted laws barring trans women from women's bathrooms at schools and some government buildings.

Metro Weekly (July 6, 2025): on June 20, 2025 Leon County Judge Lashawn Riggans threw out the trespass case against Marcy Rheintgen on a legal technicality — as a defendant charged under the Safety in Private Spaces Act she had no standing to argue the law itself was illegitimate — so the statute was never substantively tested. She had been charged March 19, 2025 after police, alerted in advance, arrested her washing her hands in a women's restroom at the Statehouse.

Equality Florida travel advisory (April 12, 2023): the organization took the 'unprecedented step' of warning about risks to the health, safety and freedom of those considering short or long-term travel or relocation to Florida, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people, reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks, and book bans/curriculum censorship. The advisory followed a wave of visitor safety inquiries; EQFL reports events and conferences cancelling and notes the US military considering redeployment for service members' families.

National law-vs-violence analysis (2008-2025 data): Florida scores 8.0 on the anti-trans law scale with 3.7 trans women murdered per 100k per year, labelled 'Do Not Travel'; the article's core finding is that state law severity does not correlate with killing rates (trendline nearly flat across the 26 states with data) — legal climate and street-level violence are independent visitor risks.

flags: 'stopped issuing corrected birth certificates' — audited sources evidence the DRIVER-LICENSE policy (SW) + a general birth-certificate-restriction concern list only; verify FL birth-cert specifics in rework

Andy Beshear's veto, enacting Senate Bill 150, which bans gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors in Kentucky and restricts which bathrooms those students can use in public schools. records.name: Montana
records.current_summary: Montana has passed laws that would grade among the country's worst — including a facility-use ban and a public-buildings bathroom ban — but state courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined them under the state constitution, leaving little of the anti-trans statutory book in force.  That makes Montana the anomaly of the 2026 legal-risk assessments: the only state whose risk grade was lowered — from 'worst laws' to 'high risk' — by cumulative court rulings and injunctions, in the February 2026 cycle. Statutory risk is high; enforcement risk is genuinely mixed.

sources.claim: July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment: Montana is flagged as a special case — it has passed laws that would normally place it among the worst states, but those laws have been repeatedly blocked or enjoined under the state constitution, improving its standing on the assessment's rubric (which ranks states by expert reading of bills on adult and youth restrictions).

National risk assessment update: Montana is the single state that improves in the 2026 rankings, because the state court system has repeatedly blocked or enjoined anti-trans laws under the state constitution; adult restrictions that were passed have not taken full effect. Youth-side picture remains unstable nationally (federal policy shifts and litigation).

records.name: Georgia
records.current_summary: A July 2026 data analysis places Georgia's recorded killing rate for trans women at 4.8 per 100k per year — among the country's highest — and a Georgia law-review article documents the long-run fatality concentration around Atlanta: at least 15 fatal cases statewide across 1990–2014 (11 in Atlanta) and 16 more across 2015–2023 (8 in Atlanta). Both series are treated by their authors as undercount floors.  The same analysis's warning applies to Georgia directly: its legal-risk grade describes how the state behaves, not how its people do — here a jurisdiction whose documented danger to trans people has been violence on the street more than legislation from the legislature.

sources.claim: The Needle (July 2026) state-by-state analysis overlaying legislative-risk maps on recorded trans-homicide data: legal risk predicts how the state treats you, not how people do; this state's recorded killing rate for trans women is 4.8 per 100k/yr — all counts acknowledged floors from an undercounted monitoring project.

Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp on March 23, 2023 signed Senate Bill 140, barring licensed medical professionals from providing patients under 18 with hormone therapy or surgery related to gender transition, with licence revocation as a possible penalty; minors who began hormone replacement therapy before July 1, 2023 may continue under the law. CNN reports the ACLU of Georgia said it would sue. The ban took effect July 1, 2023, giving an on-the-ground legal restriction relevant to a trans traveller's assessment of Georgia.

In October 2023 plaintiffs announced a settlement with Georgia's State Health Benefit Plan in Atlanta federal court, requiring the plan to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for employees, spouses and dependents, after a December 2022 lawsuit argued the plan illegally discriminated by refusing to pay. The story notes the plan could then be required to pay for care for minors outside Georgia even though prohibited inside the state. This documents that Georgia's public-employee health plan coverage for gender-affirming care continued by settlement despite the 2023 care ban.

Atlanta police said in April 2023 they were actively investigating three 'violent crimes' against transgender women in the city that year, after two Black transgender women were fatally shot a week apart; a January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition also remained open. ABC News quotes the Atlanta Police Department acknowledging the 'epidemic-level violence black and brown transgender women face in America'. The story supports the record's finding that Georgia's documented danger to trans people has been street violence concentrated in Atlanta.

Memorial Health University Medical Center in Savannah abruptly cancelled all gender-affirming surgeries on February 13, 2025, including a pre-approved double mastectomy for a 24-year-old transgender man, citing a responsibility to follow state and federal laws and regulations that appears to reference the January 28, 2025 federal executive order denying Medicare and Medicaid funding to providers of youth gender-transition care. The Current reports Savannah Pride Center said at least two other area residents were also denied care. This documents on-the-ground shrinkage of adult gender-affirming care access in Georgia under federal funding pressure.
